You extract source evidence for a paper-derived scientific benchmark. Return exactly one JSON object matching the supplied schema, with no Markdown or additional text.

Use only the fixed, line-numbered source packet. Do not use outside knowledge and do not infer an omitted coefficient, exponent, range, experimental condition, or uncertainty convention.

Extract at most one relation: the best source-supported executable quantitative relation connecting one to five numeric controls to one or two numeric readouts. A second source-reported condition is not required. Do not construct a pair, alternate world, counterfactual, task prompt, or benchmark design. If the source contains no complete relation, return {"relations":[]}.

The relation has exactly six fields: formula, parameters, controls, readouts, domain, and anchors. Formula.outputs is an executable expression tree for the source-reported central relation. Output keys must exactly match the readout names. A var leaf names a declared control and a param leaf names a declared parameter. Every declared control and parameter must occur in the formula. Numeric literals are allowed only for structural zero and one; encode every other scientific constant or fitted value as an anchored parameter. Preserve equality, approximation, fitted-relation, and asymptotic scope through the applicability statements; do not turn proportionality without its coefficient, an inequality, or an unspecified function into an exact point predictor.

A control is a numeric independent variable that can be queried within the source-supported domain. A readout is the quantitative dependent variable returned by the relation. Do not turn a latent quantity or an unreported fitted quantity into a control. Use continuous_interval only when the source supports a finite interval with minimum below maximum. Use numeric_values only for at least two explicitly supported numeric values. The domain must name every control exactly once. Record source-reported applicability or fixed context when present; otherwise use an empty applicability array.

Every formula, parameter value, control definition, readout definition, control domain, and applicability statement must carry direct inclusive source line ranges. Anchors contain line_start and line_end only. Do not generate a paraphrased support field. Use the line coordinates exactly as supplied.

Do not output source identity, schema version, an assessment, readiness flag, mechanisms, claim dependencies, ambiguity records, budget, diagnostic conditions, held-out conditions, public prose, provenance mappings, or code. Source identity and all benchmark-design fields are supplied or generated by deterministic code.

L000007	\documentclass[prl, twocolumn, floatfix]{revtex4}
L000008	\usepackage{graphicx}
L000009	\usepackage{amsmath, amsfonts, amssymb, bm}
L000010	\usepackage{braket}
L000011	\usepackage{color}
L000012	\usepackage[utf8]{inputenc}
L000013	\usepackage{mathrsfs}
L000014	\usepackage{amsbsy}

L000016	\begin{document}
L000017	
L000018	\title{ Probing atoms by periodically modulated electron bunches }
L000019	
L000020	\author{ A. B. Voitkiv$^1$, E. Schneidmiller$^2$ and T. Pfeifer$^3$}
L000021	\affiliation{ $^1$ Institute for Theoretical Physics I, Heinrich-Heine-University D\"usseldorf,
L000022	Universit\"atsstrasse 1, D-40225 D\"usseldorf, Germany \\
L000023	$^2$ Deutsches Elektronen-Synchrotron DESY, Notkestr. 85, 22607 Hamburg, Germany \\
L000024	$^3$ Max-Planck-Institut for Nuclear Physics, Saupfercheckweg 1, 69117 Heidelberg, Germany
L000025	}
L000026	
L000027	\date{\today}
L000028	
L000029	\begin{abstract}
L000030	When passing through an undulator in a Free Electron Laser,
L000031	dense bunches of relativistic electrons split into micro-bunches,
L000032	attaining a periodic space-time structure.
L000033	We show that the field of such periodically modulated bunches
L000034	is tremendously influenced by
L000035	coherence effects, resulting in a novel type of beam-atom interaction.
L000036	Our results indicate that employing such bunches
L000037	(alone or in combinations with the radiation they emit)
L000038	offers a multitude of new opportunities for exploring
L000039	atomic dynamics on a femtosecond time scale.
L000040	\end{abstract}
L000041	
L000042	\pacs{34.10+x, 34.50.Fa}
L000043	
L000044	\maketitle
L000045	
L000046	Interactions of photons and charged particles
L000047	with matter belong to the basic processes studied by
L000048	physics and results of these studies have numerous important
L000049	applications in other fields of research,
L000050	ranging from astrophysics to biology and chemistry.
L000051	
L000052	Until recently beams of charged particles (electrons, ions) had relatively low densities
L000053	and their collisions with atomic systems were driven by interactions
L000054	with individual particles of the beam \cite{Weigold}-\cite{abv_review}.
L000055	However, nowadays high-density bunches of extreme
L000056	relativistic electrons are generated by conventional
L000057	and laser or plasma wakefield
L000058	accelerators \cite{linac} - \cite{PWFA2}.
L000059	When colliding with an atomic target
L000060	a significant fraction of bunch electrons may
L000061	hit the target within its transition time.
L000062	As a result, these electrons could coherently interact
L000063	with the target, that strongly affects the target dynamics \cite{we-2025}.
L000064	
L000065	In a Free Electron Laser (FEL) a dense bunch of highly relativistic electrons from
L000066	a linear accelerator passes through an undulator, generating nearly monochromatic
L000067	intense radiation \cite{FEL1}-\cite{fel-book}.
L000068	When passing through an undulator the bunch  --
L000069	due to the interaction with the magnetic field of the undulator and
L000070	the emitted radiation -- splits into micro-bunches, attaining a periodic space-time structure
L000071	of a 'diffraction grating' which moves with an extreme relativistic velocity.
L000072	According to our estimates, depending on the bunch and undulator parameters,
L000073	the 'diffraction grating' may keep its shape over distances
L000074	$ \sim 1 - 10 $ m after leaving the undulator.
L000075	
L000076	In this communication we show that, due to exceptional properties of such 'grating'-projectiles
L000077	-- a periodic structure, a large number (up to $ \sim 10^6 $ - $ 10^7 $) of electrons
L000078	in a micro-bunch and a very short ($\lesssim 100 $ as) micro-bunch
L000079	duration, their collisions with atoms are driven by
L000080	a novel type of a beam-atom interaction.
L000081	Its novelty originates in a multi-level coherence,
L000082	where a coherent action of the micro-bunches re-shapes the high-frequency
L000083	part of the bunch field into nearly monochromatic lines, whose intensity
L000084	is strongly amplified by a coherent action of electrons within each micro-bunch,
L000085	and a coherent action of the entire bunch
L000086	creates an extreme intense
L000087	maximum at low frequencies. Exploiting this interaction
L000088	offers new opportunities for exploring atomic dynamics on very short time scales.
L000089	
L000090	The field of a highly relativistic charged particle
L000091	can be though of as consisting of the so called 'equivalent photons' \cite{equiv-ph}-\cite{jack}.
L000092	We will show that the high-frequency part of the bunch-atom interaction is
L000093	transmitted by coherent equivalent (CE) photons
L000094	whose energies coincide with energies of the real photons
L000095	emitted by the bunch in the undulator and whose intensities
L000096	can be made close to those of the real photons.
L000097	
L000098	Let the target atom, which is at rest in the laboratory frame,
L000099	be bombarded by a bunch of extreme relativistic electrons.
L000100	The bunch electrons move in the laboratory frame with a velocity $\bm v$ along
L000101	the $z$-axis, $\bm v = (0,0,v)$. We shall suppose that the bunch
L000102	was modulated along this axis that transformed it into
L000103	a train of equidistantly separated
L000104	micro-bunches with a similar shape.
L000105	
L000106	The cross section  $ \frac{ d \sigma_{\rm fi}}{ d^2 \bm q_\perp } $
L000107	for atomic transition, differential in the transverse momentum transfer
L000108	$\bm q_{\perp}$ ($ \bm q_{\perp} \cdot \bm v = 0 $) to the atom,
L000109	is given by
L000110	\begin{eqnarray}
L000111	\frac{ d \sigma_{\rm fi}}{ d^2 \bm q_\perp }  & = &
L000112	\frac{ d \sigma^{\rm (1 \, el)}_{\rm fi}}{ d^2 \bm q_\perp }
L000113	\times \Big \{ \vert F(\bm q) \vert^2  +  N_t \Big \}.
L000114	\label{v1}
L000115	\end{eqnarray}
L000116	Here, $\frac{ d \sigma^{\rm (1 \, el)}_{\rm fi}}{ d^2 \bm q_\perp }$  is the cross section in the collision
L000117	with a single electron from the bunch. It reads
L000118	\begin{eqnarray}
L000119	\frac{ d \sigma^{\rm(1 \, el)}_{\rm fi}}{ d^2 \bm q_\perp } \! = \!
L000120	\frac{ 4 \, e_0^4 }{ \hbar^2 v^2 } \frac{ \big \vert \langle \psi_{\rm f} |
L000121	e^{i \bm q \cdot \bm r} \!
L000122	- \!\! \frac{ v }{ 2 m_e c^2 } \! \big( \! e^{i \bm q \cdot \bm r} \hat{p}_z \! + \!
L000123	\hat{p}_z e^{i \bm q \cdot \bm r} \big)
L000124	\vert \psi_{\rm i} \rangle \big \vert^2 }
L000125	{\left( \bm q^2 - \frac{ \omega_{\rm fi}^2}{c^2}
L000126	\right)^2 },
L000127	\label{em2}
L000128	\end{eqnarray}
L000129	where $e_0$ and $m_e$ are the electron charge and mass, respectively,
L000130	$\bm r = (x,y,z)$ is the coordinate of the atomic electron with respect
L000131	to the atomic nucleus,  $\hat{p}_z = \frac{ \hbar }{ i } \frac{\partial }{ \partial z } $,
L000132	$\psi_{\rm i}$ and $\varepsilon_{\rm i}$
L000133	($\psi_{\rm f}$ and $\varepsilon_{\rm f}$)
L000134	are the initial (final) atomic state and its energy, respectively,
L000135	$\omega_{\rm fi} = (\varepsilon_{\rm f} - \varepsilon_{\rm i})/\hbar$ is the atomic transition frequency,
L000136	$ \hbar \bm q = (\hbar \bm q_\perp, \hbar q_\parallel) $ is the momentum transfer to the atom,
L000137	$\hbar q_\parallel = \hbar \omega_{\rm fi}/v $ is the minimum momentum transfer
L000138	and $c$ is the speed of light.
L000139	
L000140	Further, $ N_t $ is the total number of electrons in the bunch
L000141	and $ F(\bm q) $ is the elastic form-factor of the bunch,
L000142	\begin{eqnarray}
L000143	F(\bm q)  & = &
L000144	\int \!\!d^3 {\bm R } \, \,
L000145	\rho( \bm R) \, \,
L000146	e^{ - i \bm q \cdot \bm R },
L000147	\label{v3}
L000148	\end{eqnarray}
L000149	where $ \rho( \bm R) $ is
L000150	the bunch density and the integration runs over the
L000151	bunch volume \cite{fixed-time}.
L000152	In (\ref{v1}) the terms $ \sim N_t $ and $ \sim \vert F(\bm q) \vert^2 $
L000153	correspond to the independent (incoherent) and coherent, respectively, action
L000154	of the bunch electrons in the collision.
L000155	The coherent channel may become very efficient
L000156	when there is a large number of electrons in
L000157	the coherence volume $ V_c \simeq \frac{ \pi }{ q_\perp^2 q_\parallel } $ \cite{we-2025}.
L000158	
L000159	If the bunch is a train of equidistantly separated
L000160	micro-bunches with a similar shape, we obtain
L000161	\begin{eqnarray}
L000162	F(\bm q)  & = & \mathcal{F}(\bm q)  \, \,  \mathcal{G}(\bm q),
L000163	\label{v4}
L000164	\end{eqnarray}
L000165	where
L000166	\begin{eqnarray}
L000167	\mathcal{F}(\bm q) = \int \!\!d^3 {\bm R } \, \,
L000168	\rho_0( \bm R) \, \,
L000169	e^{ - i \bm q \cdot \bm R }
L000170	\label{v5}
L000171	\end{eqnarray}
L000172	is the elastic form-factor of a single micro-bunch
L000173	with the density $ \rho_0( \bm R) $ and
L000174	\begin{eqnarray}
L000175	\mathcal{G}(\bm q) = \sum_{ k } f_{k,0} \, e^{ - i \, k \, q_\parallel \, \mathcal{L}}
L000176	\label{v6}
L000177	\end{eqnarray}
L000178	is the structure factor of the bunch. In (\ref{v6})
L000179	the sum runs over the micro-bunches, $\mathcal{L}$
L000180	is the distance between them and
L000181	$f_{k,0}$ are coefficients
L000182	describing the relative intensities of the micro-bunches.
L000183	This factor arises due to the interference
L000184	between the contributions to the atomic transition
L000185	amplitude from the interaction with different micro-bunches.
L000186	Its form closely resembles that of the factor describing
L000187	a multi-slit interference of light scattered off a diffraction grating.
L000188	In our case the effective 'grating' arises due to a periodic structure
L000189	of the electron bunch \cite{rest-frame}.
L000190	
L000191	The factor $ \vert \mathcal{G} \vert^2 $ reaches its maximum
L000192	at $ q_\parallel \, \mathcal{L} = 2 \pi n$, where
L000193	$n = 1, 2, 3, ...$ which corresponds to resonant frequencies,
L000194	$ \omega_{n} = \frac{2 \pi }{ \mathcal{T} } \, n$, where
L000195	$ \mathcal{T}  = \mathcal{ L }/v $
L000196	is the time interval between the arrival of two consecutive micro-bunches.
L000197	When the number of the  micro-bunches is very large and
L000198	$f_{k,0}$ varies slowly with $k$, $ \vert \mathcal{G} \vert^2 $ strongly peaks at
L000199	the resonant frequencies.
L000200	
L000201	\vspace{0.25cm}
L000202	
L000203	In what follows we shall consider electron bunches by relying on
L000204	parameters of two high-repetition-rate superconducting FEL facilities,
L000205	FLASH \cite{FLASH} and the European XFEL \cite{EuXFEL}.
L000206	The former, which is driven by bunches with electron energies $ 0.5$ - $1.35$ GeV,  operates in the XUV and soft x-ray regimes and comprises two undulator lines.
L000207	One of these has been upgraded to a high-repetition-rate seeded FEL line \cite{high-rep}
L000208	and is expected to deliver fully coherent photon pulses for user operation in the near future.
L000209	For simplicity, we consider a special regime
L000210	proposed to improve seeding performance,
L000211	namely two-bunch seeding \cite{two-bunch-seed},
L000212	in which only the fundamental harmonic
L000213	of the FEL undulator is imprinted
L000214	on the electron bunch \cite{many-harmon}.
L000215	
L000216	Let us consider the ionization of H(1s) atoms by a (FLASH) electron bunch
L000217	with an electron energy of $1.35$ GeV,
L000218	a total charge of 250
L000219	pC (corresponding to $ N_t = 1.6 \times 10^9$  electrons) and a
L000220	bunch length of $L = 30 $ $\mu$m. The bunch passed through
L000221	a linearly polarized undulator with the period $ \lambda_U = 3.5 $ cm
L000222	and deflection parameter $ \mathcal{ K } = 3.8$.
L000223	With an average beta function of $7$ m in the undulator
L000224	and the normalized emittance \cite{linac}
L000225	$0.5$ mm$ \cdot $mrad,
L000226	the bunch radius is $ a_0 = \sqrt{2} \sigma_x = 51$ $\mu$m.
L000227	In the undulator
L000228	the electron bunch splits into micro-bunches
L000229	separated along the bunch propagation by the fundamental wavelength
L000230	of the emitted radiation \cite{FEL1}.
L000231	As our estimates show,
L000232	after leaving the undulator the bunch keeps this periodic structure
L000233	over distances of several meters.
L000234	
L000235	We shall assume that the shape of the electron micro-bunches is Gaussian,
L000236	\begin{eqnarray}
L000237	\rho_{k}( \bm R) = \frac{ \mathcal{N}_k }{ \pi^{3/2} \, \, a_0^2 \, l_0   } \,
L000238	\, e^{- Z^2/l_0^2 }  \, \, e^{ - R_\perp^2/a_0^2},
L000239	\label{v7}
L000240	\end{eqnarray}
L000241	where $ \mathcal{N}_k $ is the number of electrons in the $k$-th micro-bunch, and
L000242	$ l_0 $ and $ a_0 $ are the effective length and radius, respectively,
L000243	of the micro-bunches \cite{rms}. The coefficients $ f_{k,0} $ in (\ref{v5})
L000244	are chosen to reflect the Gaussian longitudinal profile of the entire bunch.
L000245	
L000246	The chosen bunch parameters result in the value of
L000247	$ \lambda_1 \approx 2 \times 10^{-6} $   cm for
L000248	the fundamental wavelength, given by
L000249	$ \lambda_1 = \frac{ \lambda_U }{ 2 \gamma^2 } (1 + 0.5 \, \mathcal{ K }^2) $
L000250	\cite{FEL1},
L000251	for the electromagnetic radiation emitted by
L000252	the bunch along its propagation direction.
L000253	The fundamental frequency $\omega_1 = \frac{2 \pi \, v}{ \lambda_1 } $
L000254	corresponds to the energy $ \hbar \, \omega_1 \approx 60 $ eV.
L000255	We further obtain that the effective number
L000256	of the micro-bunches $ \simeq L/\lambda_1  = 2 \times 10^3 $ and
L000257	the number $\mathcal{N}_k$ of electrons in the most intense micro-bunches is
L000258	$ \simeq 7 \times 10^5 $. The length $l_0$ of a micro-bunch is proportional to
L000259	$ \lambda_1 $: $l_0 = \eta \, \lambda_1 $. We take $\eta = 0.25$, which yields
L000260	$ l_0 \simeq  5 \times 10^{-7}$ cm
L000261	(the corresponding micro-bunch duration is $ \approx 17 $ as).
L000262	
L000263	\begin{figure}[t]
L000264	\vspace{-0.5cm}
L000265	\begin{center}
L000266	\includegraphics[width=0.40\textwidth]{H-ionization.png}
L000267	\end{center}
L000268	\vspace{-0.95cm}
L000269	\caption{ Energy spectrum of electrons emitted in ionization of H(1s) atoms
L000270	by a bunch of $1.35$ GeV electrons passed through an undulator.
L000271	$N_t = 1.6 \times 10^{9}$, $ L = 30 $ $\mu$m, $a_0 = 50 $ $\mu$m,
L000272	$ \lambda_U = 3.5 $ cm, $\mathcal{ K } = 3.8 $ and
L000273	$l_0 = 0.005 $ $\mu$m.
L000274	Dotted curve: all bunch electrons act incoherently (multipled by $10$).
L000275	Dashed curve: coherence within a micro-bunch is taken into account
L000276	but the micro-bunches act incoherently.
L000277	Solid curve: coherences within a single micro-bunch and of different micro-bunches
L000278	are taken into account. The cross sections are given {\bf per bunch}.
L000279	}
L000280	\vspace{-0.1cm}
L000281	\label{figure1}
L000282	\end{figure}
L000283	
L000284	In figure \ref{figure1} we present results of three different calculations
L000285	for the energy spectrum of the emitted electrons.
L000286	
L000287	i) The dotted curve was
L000288	obtained by assuming that all
L000289	$1.6 \times 10^{9}$ bunch electrons interact with the hydrogen atoms
L000290	individually (in order to make this spectrum more visible,
L000291	in the figure it was multiplied by $10$).
L000292	
L000293	ii) The dashed curve accounts for
L000294	the coherent action of the electrons within each
L000295	micro-bunch but assumes that the
L000296	micro-bunches act incoherently.
L000297	
L000298	iii) The solid curve was obtained
L000299	by taking into account the coherent action not only
L000300	within each micro-bunch but also
L000301	across all micro-bunches.
L000302	
L000303	Figure \ref{figure1} demonstrates that the coherence within a micro-bunch
L000304	strongly enhances the ionization process whereas the coherent action of the
L000305	micro-bunches drastically changes the shape of the emission spectrum by
L000306	compressing it into sharp peaks separated by
L000307	the energy $ 2 \pi \hbar \, \frac{ v }{ \lambda_1 } $.
L000308	This points to the presence of strong (quasi-) monochromatic lines
L000309	$ \omega_n = \frac{2 \pi \, v}{ \lambda_1 } \, n$ ($n = 1,2,3,...$)
L000310	in the energy spectrum of the CE photons
L000311	carried by the electron bunch passed through the undulator.
L000312	
L000313	\begin{figure}[t]
L000314	\vspace{-0.25cm}
L000315	\begin{center}
L000316	\includegraphics[width=0.40\textwidth]{virt-photons-a-new.png}
L000317	\end{center}
L000318	\vspace{-0.95cm}
L000319	\caption{ The energy spectrum of equivalent photons
L000320	carried by $1.35$ GeV (solid curve) and $ 14 $ GeV (dash curve) electron bunches
L000321	(for each bunch only the first two high-frequency lines are shown). The spectrum
L000322	of equivalent photons, carried by the corresponding unmodulated bunches,
L000323	are shown by squares.
L000324	For more explanations see text.
L000325	}
L000326	\vspace{-0.1cm}
L000327	\label{figure2}
L000328	\end{figure}
L000329	
L000330	In figure \ref{figure2} we show the energy spectrum
L000331	of equivalent photons for two electron bunches. One of them is
L000332	the bunch considered above. The other can be operated at
L000333	the European XFEL, which produces coherent x-ray radiation at three undulator lines driven
L000334	by a high-energy electron bunch with energies up to $16.3$ GeV. The line SASE3 operates
L000335	in the soft-x-ray regime, enabled by its large undulator period of $\lambda_U = 6.8$ cm
L000336	and high deflection parameter. We consider an electron energy
L000337	of $14$ GeV and $\mathcal{K} = 7.2$,
L000338	resulting in a photon energy of $ \approx 1 $ keV. The electron bunch parameters
L000339	are the same as in the FLASH example, except for a shorter length of $ 10 $ $\mu$m
L000340	and a smaller radius $ a_0 = 24 $ $\mu$m (assuming
L000341	an average beta function of $16$ m in the undulator).
L000342	The considered undulator line operates in
L000343	the self-amplified spontaneous emission (SASE) regime, which provides only partial longitudinal
L000344	coherence \cite{fel-book}.
L000345	Full longitudinal coherence can be achieved using a self-seeding scheme
L000346	\cite{feldhaus}, \cite{ratner}.
L000347	Here, for illustration, we consider the fully coherent case \cite{f-SASE}.
L000348	
L000349	Two main features of the photon spectrum
L000350	are seen in figure
L000351	\ref{figure2}: (i) narrow high-frequency lines of
L000352	CE photons
L000353	(for each bunch only the first two are shown),
L000354	whose positions practically coincide with those
L000355	of the real photons emitted in the undulator (not shown), and
L000356	(ii) an extremely intense maximum at very low energies,
L000357	$ \hbar \omega_{\rm ph} \lesssim \hbar v/L $.
L000358	
L000359	The analysis shows that the integral intensity
L000360	of each high-frequency line is inversely
L000361	proportional to the length $L$ of
L000362	the electron bunch and that the dependence on
L000363	the bunch radius $a_0$ is more complicated,
L000364	varying from $ \sim a_0^{-4} $ at $ a_0  \gg v \gamma/ \omega_n  $
L000365	to $ \sim \ln(1/a_0) $ at $ a_0  \ll v \gamma/ \omega_n  $. The
L000366	$a_0$-dependence is illustrated in figure \ref{figure3}.

L000368	\vspace{-0.5cm}
L000369	\begin{center}
L000370	\includegraphics[width=0.40\textwidth]{a0_dependence_logarithm.png}
L000371	\end{center}
L000372	\vspace{-0.95cm}
L000373	\caption{ The number of CE photons in the line centered at
L000374	$\hbar \omega_1 \approx 60$ eV
L000375	as a function of the bunch radius $a_0$.
L000376	The other parameters are $N_t = 1.6 \times 10^9$,  $1.35$ GeV,
L000377	$ L = 30 $ $\mu$m, $ \lambda_U = 3.5 $ cm, $\mathcal{ K } = 3.8 $ and
L000378	$l_0 = 0.005 $ $\mu$m.
L000379	}
L000380	\vspace{-0.1cm}
L000381	\label{figure3}
L000382	\end{figure}
L000383	
L000384	\vspace{0.15cm}
L000385	
L000386	The maximum at very low frequencies
L000387	contains equivalent
L000388	photons with wavelengths
L000389	comparable or exceeding the bunch length $L$ and, therefore,
L000390	its shape \cite{1bunch} is not sensitive to micro-bunching
L000391	(see figure \ref{figure2}).
L000392	This maximum is so extreme intense because
L000393	the entire bunch coherently contributes to it,
L000394	making its intensity proportional to $N_t^2$.
L000395	
L000396	Our calculations for the photon spectrum differential in
L000397	the distance $b$ from the bunch axis show that
L000398	even very large $b$ ($b > 100 \, a_0$, \cite{vacuum-chamber}) noticeably contribute
L000399	to the low-frequency maximum. Therefore, its enormous intensity
L000400	does not necessarily imply
L000401	strong fields because the low-frequency photons
L000402	are spread over a large volume.
L000403	
L000404	Single-pulse (unmodulated) electron bunches, whose duration greatly exceeds
L000405	typical atomic times
L000406	($ \tau_A \simeq 24 $ as),
L000407	can ionize atoms via
L000408	individual-electron---atom collisions and tunneling.
L000409	Tunneling is a coherent mechanism
L000410	but differs qualitatively from coherent impact ionization \cite{we-2025},
L000411	which is efficient for short ($ \lesssim  10 \, \tau_A$)
L000412	single-pulse bunches, proceeding
L000413	via absorption of equivalent photons whose energy exceed
L000414	the atomic binding energy.
L000415	
L000416	As our calculations show,
L000417	for the bunch parameters in figures \ref{figure1}
L000418	the tunneling ionization of H(1s) is negligible.
L000419	However, since the tunneling ionization rate,
L000420	$\sim \frac{F_a}{F} \exp(-2 F_a / 3 F) $ \cite{LL-III}
L000421	($F$ is the low-frequency bunch field and $F_a \sim 10^9$ V/cm
L000422	is the characteristic atomic field), strongly depends on $F$,
L000423	this mechanism is extremely sensitive to
L000424	the bunch parameters \cite{we-2025}.
L000425	We also note that long before the bunch field reaches values,
L000426	where the tunneling becomes possible,
L000427	it can already efficiently mix closely lying bound atomic states.
L000428	
L000429	The contributions of tunneling \cite{tun1}-\cite{tun2},
L000430	absorption of high-frequency CE photons
L000431	and collisions with individual electrons to the ionization of H(1s) by the $14$ GeV
L000432	bunch are shown in figure \ref{figure4}. There we see an enormous increase
L000433	in the tunneling ionization with decreasing $a_0$ and
L000434	inefficiency of ionization via absorption
L000435	of the CE photons because
L000436	their energies ($ \gtrsim 1 $ keV) greatly exceed the hydrogen
L000437	binding energy ($\approx 13.6$ eV), making the absorpsion unlikely.
L000438	
L000439	\begin{figure}[t]
L000440	\vspace{-0.5cm}
L000441	\begin{center}
L000442	\includegraphics[width=0.40\textwidth]{a0_tunneling.png}
L000443	\end{center}
L000444	\vspace{-0.95cm}
L000445	\caption{ Ionization of H(1s) by $14$ GeV electron bunch as a function of
L000446	the bunch radius. $N_t = 1.6 \times 10^9$,
L000447	$ L = 10 $ $\mu$m, $ \lambda_U = 6.8 $ cm, $\mathcal{ K } = 7.2 $.

L000449	ionization by $N_t$ individual electrons. Dotted curve: ionization
L000450	via absorption of a CE photon from
L000451	the first high-frequency line.
L000452	}
L000453	\vspace{-0.1cm}

L000455	\end{figure}
L000456	
L000457	\vspace{0.15cm}
L000458	
L000459	Thus, an electron bunch,
L000460	passed through an undulator,
L000461	carries an electromagnetic field, where
L000462	nearly monochromatic high-frequency CE photons
L000463	'co-exist' with a field that slowly varies in time.
L000464	Such a -- perfectly synchronized --  field combination
L000465	can, for instance, be used for exploring many-electron atoms
L000466	where inner and outer electrons are accessed via
L000467	the high-frequency photons and the low-frequency field, respectively,
L000468	or studying non-dipole transitions
L000469	in hydrogen-like ions via resonant absorption of
L000470	a high-frequency CE photon and coupling of nearly
L000471	degenerate excited states by the low-frequency field.
L000472	
L000473	Intensities of high-frequency CE photons
L000474	can be further strongly enhanced
L000475	by reducing the radius of the electron bunch.
L000476	This can, for instance, be done by installing
L000477	at the undulator exit a compact chicane with a photon-beam deflector,
L000478	followed by a quadrupole triplet that focuses
L000479	the electron beam by a factor of $\simeq 4$,
L000480	corresponding to a beta function at the waist
L000481	of $0.5$ m. The total length of the system would only be a few meters.
L000482	
L000483	Our estimates show that for both electron bunches under consideration
L000484	the radius can be reduced by $4$-$5$ times without
L000485	spoiling their periodic structure. This increases
L000486	the intensity of high-frequency CE photon lines by two orders of magnitude
L000487	(for an illustration see figure \ref{figure3}).
L000488	
L000489	\vspace{0.15cm}
L000490	
L000491	The high-frequency CE photons closely resemble the field
L000492	of the emitted radiation. However,
L000493	important differences still hold,
L000494	including a fundamental one: unlike for a real photon field,
L000495	the integral $\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \bm E_{\perp} dt $
L000496	(where $ \bm E_{\perp} $ is the transverse part of the electric field)
L000497	does not vanish for the CE photon field. Also,
L000498	polarization properties can be quite different \cite{polariz}.
L000499	This, in general, implies additional differences
L000500	in the response of atomic systems
L000501	when they are probed by real and equivalent photons
L000502	produced by the same electron bunch.
L000503	
L000504	By separating the electron bunch from the emitted radiation
L000505	at the undulator exit (while preserving its density modulation),
L000506	the bunch can be used for probing atomic systems on a fs time scale.
L000507	Several approaches for implementing such a separation
L000508	have been considered  \cite{ES-6},
L000509	including an achromatic bend or a compact chicane combined with an
L000510	absorber or deflector for the radiation.
L000511	
L000512	A key advantage of the electron beams over real photon beams generated at XFEL
L000513	facilities is the ability to combine multiple spectral components
L000514	within a single pulse. Beyond the combination of high- and low-frequency components,
L000515	additional intermediate frequency bands can be produced through laser-based manipulation
L000516	in XFEL injectors \cite{new-1,new-2}, two-color seeding schemes \cite{new-3}
L000517	with frequency-mixing techniques \cite{new-4},
L000518	or controlled shaping of the electron density distribution
L000519	in bunch compressors \cite{FLASH}.
L000520	
L000521	Moreover, distinct spectral components can be generated in different temporal slices of the
L000522	same electron bunch with a controllable delay, enabling pump–probe measurements
L000523	within a single shot. A related pump–probe concept employing real photons and
L000524	a short ($\simeq 250$ as) broad-band single-pulse electron bunch was proposed
L000525	in \cite{cesar}. However, in the present scheme all spectral components
L000526	can be realized using equivalent photons alone.
L000527	This unified approach simplifies the experimental layout
L000528	and facilitates rapid re-configuration between different measurement modes.
L000529	
L000530	One can also probe atomic systems
L000531	by various coherent combinations of CE photons with
L000532	the emitted radiation.
L000533	Here various scenarios are possible.
L000534	For instance, one can shift azimuthal symmetry axes
L000535	of beams of equivalent and real photons
L000536	with respect to each other, producing
L000537	a high-frequency field with non-trivial polarization.
L000538	Beams of equivalent and real photons can
L000539	also be combined at different angles,
L000540	enabling multiwave mixing \cite{new-5},
L000541	controlled interference effects,
L000542	and the generation of complex polarization structures.
L000543	
L000544	\vspace{0.25cm}
L000545	
L000546	In conclusion, in FELs, bunches of extreme relativistic electrons
L000547	pass through an undulator, attaining a periodic space-time structure
L000548	that may survive over considerable distances after leaving the undulator.
L000549	We have shown that the interaction of such bunches with atoms
L000550	is tremendously modified by multi-level coherence effects,
L000551	where a coherent action of the micro-bunches
L000552	re-shapes the high-frequency part of the bunch field into nearly
L000553	monochromatic lines, a coherent action of electrons within each micro-bunch
L000554	strongly amplifies intensities of these lines and
L000555	a confluence of these two coherences occurs at low frequencies,
L000556	resulting in an extreme intense
L000557	maximum, created by a coherent action of the entire bunch.
L000558	
L000559	In FELs, electron bunches are employed for generating
L000560	electromagnetic radiation.
L000561	Our results indicate that such bunches can further be exploited
L000562	(alone or in coherent combinations with the radiation they emit),
L000563	offering  a multitude of new opportunities for exploring
L000564	atomic dynamics on a femtosecond time scale.
